hero.label: extropy · web development
hero.lede: I'm Maksim, a fullstack developer. I build complete web products: online stores, booking platforms, delivery services and product sites. Payments add up to the cent, accounts stay secure, and every screen size is treated as first class.

principles.label: The five petals
principles.title: The name is a promise. The logo is its diagram.
principles.intro: Extropy is the opposite of entropy: order that grows instead of decaying. The philosophy behind the word rests on five principles, and the lotus in my mark carries five petals, one for each. Here is what they mean when I build for you.

items.name: Perpetual Progress
items.essence: Relentless self-improvement and the pursuit of knowledge. Never settling for the level already reached.
items.practice: Your codebase never rots: dependencies stay current, patterns get revisited, and every project I ship is measurably better engineered than the one before it.

items.name: Self-Transformation
items.essence: Deliberately becoming someone more capable, with science, technology and honest work on yourself.
items.practice: I started in C++ and game engines and rebuilt myself into a fullstack web developer. I'll learn whatever your problem actually needs. The stack serves the problem, never the reverse.

items.name: Practical Optimism
items.essence: A constructive view of the future: problems exist to be solved, not endured or dramatized.
items.practice: You never hear "that's impossible". You hear "here's the trade-off, here's my recommendation, here's the plan". And then it ships.

items.name: Open Society
items.essence: Openness to critique and dialogue, the absence of dogma. Ideas win on merit.
items.practice: You see the repository, the estimates, and the reasoning behind them. Questions get straight answers, and "because I said so" is never an argument.

items.name: Smart Technology
items.essence: Technology as a lever: innovation that extends what people can do.
items.practice: Proven, boring tech where reliability matters, new tech only where it pays for itself. Every dependency in your project earns its place.

notes.label: Field notes
notes.title: The five things clients worry about
notes.intro: Every note takes a real fear, like lost payments, leaked accounts or vanishing carts, and shows exactly how I make it a non-issue.

stack.label: The stack
stack.title: Few tools, deeply known
stack.intro: I'd rather master seven tools than dabble in seventy. This is the set I build with every day, and why each one earned its place.

items.name: Next.js
items.why: One framework for the whole product: server rendering, streaming, API routes. The fastest path from idea to production quality.

items.name: TypeScript
items.why: Every line typed. Whole categories of bugs become impossible before the code even runs.

items.name: Tailwind CSS
items.why: Design tokens enforced by the compiler. The interface stays one interface, no matter how many hands touch it.

items.name: Supabase
items.why: Postgres with auth and row-level security built in. The database itself becomes the last line of defense.

items.name: Drizzle ORM
items.why: SQL with full type safety: the schema lives in code, migrations are reviewable, and queries can't reference what doesn't exist.

items.name: Zustand + React Query
items.why: Client state and server state are different problems. Each gets the right tool instead of one store doing both badly.

items.name: Stripe
items.why: The money layer, integrated the way Stripe's own docs wish everyone did it: webhooks, idempotency, reconciliation.

about.label: The person
about.title: Maksim, the person behind extropy
about.lede: Nineteen years old, from Odesa, building from the Netherlands. Web developer with a path that started inside a post-apocalyptic video game.

story.heading: How I got here
body: At thirteen I found The Last of Us, and it rewired me. It wasn't just a game. It was proof that software could carry a story that hits like a film. I wanted to build worlds like that, so I learned the language they're built in: C++.

C++ took me to Unreal Engine, C# took me to Unity, and a series of pet projects taught me what engines teach best: how complex systems fit together, and why they fall apart. Somewhere between those projects I noticed where my time actually went. Not gameplay, but interfaces, logic, structure. The web had all of that, plus something games didn't: real people using what you built, immediately.

In 2024 the war made the geography decision for me: the college where I studied in Odesa was destroyed. I moved to the Netherlands, enrolled in software development at MBO Amersfoort, and kept building in a new country and a new language. That's when extropy stopped being a nice word and became the way I work: order that grows, against everything pulling the other way.

items.title: The spark
items.body: The Last of Us shows me what software can make people feel. I start learning C++ to build worlds of my own.

items.title: Game engines
items.body: C++ with Unreal Engine, then C# with Unity. Pet projects that teach systems thinking, performance budgets, and finishing what you start.

items.title: The turn to the web
items.body: Beautiful sites and smart applications pull me in. I commit to the fullstack path: React, Next.js, and everything around them.

items.title: Odesa → Amersfoort
items.body: My college in Odesa is destroyed in the war. I move to the Netherlands and continue as a software development student at MBO Amersfoort, without missing a beat.

items.title: extropy
items.body: Shipped projects: an e-commerce store, a booking platform, a delivery service, product sites. The brand gets its name, its lotus, and this site.

languages.heading: Four languages, daily
languages.intro: Communication is part of engineering. I work with clients directly in all four, no translator in the middle.

why.heading: Why "extropy"
why.body: Entropy is decay: systems drifting toward disorder. Extropy is the opposite pull, intelligence and deliberate effort making things better over time. Five principles, five petals on the lotus, and the standard every project gets held to.

contact.label: Contact
contact.title: Tell me what you're building
contact.lede: A shop that has to sell, an app that has to work, or an idea that needs an honest technical opinion. Write to me in any of my four languages.

process.heading: What working with me looks like
process.intro: No mystery, no disappearing acts. Four steps, each ending with something you can see.

items.title: We talk
items.body: You describe the goal in plain words. I ask the questions that surface the real requirements, which is usually more useful than the brief itself.

items.title: You get a plan
items.body: Scope, stages, an honest timeline, and what each stage costs. If something is risky, you hear it now, not in week six.

items.title: I build, you watch
items.body: Short iterations with something clickable at the end of each one. The repository is yours from day one.

items.title: Launch isn't goodbye
items.body: You get a documented, maintainable codebase, and I stay around to make sure it survives contact with real users.
